locator: Internal organization of NumPy arrays, opening paragraph
claim: An ndarray is a data buffer plus metadata describing that buffer, and the buffer itself is a contiguous, fixed block of fixed-size items.
quote: NumPy arrays consist of two major components: the raw array data (from now on, referred to as the data buffer), and the information about the raw array data. The data buffer is typically what people think of as arrays in C or Fortran, a contiguous (and fixed) block of memory containing fixed-sized data items.

locator: Internal organization of NumPy arrays, numbered list of descriptive information, items 1-4
claim: The metadata records the element size in bytes, the start of the data as an offset into the buffer, the number of dimensions with their sizes, and a per-dimension stride that need not be a multiple of the element size.
quote:
1.  The basic data element’s size in bytes.

2.  The start of the data within the data buffer (an offset relative to the beginning of the data buffer).

3.  The number of dimensions and the size of each dimension.

4.  The separation between elements for each dimension (the stride). This does not have to be a multiple of the element size.

locator: The N-dimensional array (ndarray), section 'Internal memory layout of an ndarray', paragraph beginning 'In a strided scheme'
claim: In a strided scheme an N-dimensional index maps to a byte offset equal to the sum over axes of index times stride, measured from the beginning of the memory block, with integer strides.
quote:
In a strided scheme, the N-dimensional index \((n_0, n_1, ..., n_{N-1})\) corresponds to the offset (in bytes):

\[n_{\mathrm{offset}} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} s_k n_k\]

from the beginning of the memory block associated with the array. Here, \(s_k\) are integers which specify the strides of the array.

locator: The N-dimensional array (ndarray), section 'Internal memory layout of an ndarray', note item 1 on strides that may differ from the canonical ones
claim: An axis of length one admits only index zero, so that axis's stride never contributes to an offset and its value is arbitrary.
quote: If self.shape[k] == 1 then for any legal index index[k] == 0. This means that in the formula for the offset \(n_k = 0\) and thus \(s_k n_k = 0\) and the value of \(s_k\) = self.strides[k] is arbitrary.

locator: The N-dimensional array (ndarray), section 'Internal memory layout of an ndarray', paragraph after the row and column stride formulas
claim: C order and Fortran order are both contiguous layouts, meaning single-segment memory in which every part of the memory block is reachable by some combination of the indices.
quote: Both the C and Fortran orders are contiguous, i.e., single-segment, memory layouts, in which every part of the memory block can be accessed by some combination of the indices.

locator: Copies and views, section 'View', first paragraph
claim: A view is made by changing metadata only over the same data buffer, so changes made to a view are visible in the original array.
quote: It is possible to access the array differently by just changing certain metadata like stride and dtype without changing the data buffer. This creates a new way of looking at the data and these new arrays are called views. The data buffer remains the same, so any changes made to a view reflects in the original copy.

locator: Indexing on ndarrays, section 'Basic slicing and indexing', paragraph on view results
claim: Every array produced by basic slicing is a view of the original array.
quote: All arrays generated by basic slicing are always views of the original array.

locator: Copies and views, section 'Copy', first paragraph
claim: A copy duplicates both the data buffer and the metadata, so changes made to the copy do not affect the original array.
quote: When a new array is created by duplicating the data buffer as well as the metadata, it is called a copy. Changes made to the copy do not reflect on the original array. Making a copy is slower and memory-consuming but sometimes necessary. A copy can be forced by using ndarray.copy.

locator: Internal organization of NumPy arrays, paragraph beginning 'Other operations, such as transpose'
claim: Transpose does not move data elements; it changes the shape and stride information so that indexing changes while the data stays in place.
quote: Other operations, such as transpose, don’t move data elements around in the array, but rather change the information about the shape and strides so that the indexing of the array changes, but the data in the array doesn’t move.

claim: For a basic slice NumPy takes start, stop, step and length from PySlice_GetIndicesEx, advances the data pointer by stride times start, multiplies the axis stride by step, and sets the axis length to that number of steps; a non-positive length is turned into an empty axis.

locator: Indexing on ndarrays, section 'Basic slicing and indexing', first bullet on slice syntax
claim: For a basic slice, the selected indices are i, i + k, ..., i + (m - 1)k, where m = q + (r != 0) and q and r are the quotient and remainder of j - i divided by k, so the last selected index stays below j.
quote: This selects the m elements (in the corresponding dimension) with index values i, i + k, …, i + (m - 1) k where \(m = q + (r\neq0)\) and q and r are the quotient and remainder obtained by dividing j - i by k: j - i = q k + r, so that i + (m - 1) k < j.

locator: Indexing on ndarrays, section 'Basic slicing and indexing', second bullet on negative indices and steps
claim: In basic slicing a negative start or stop index is interpreted as n plus that index, and a negative step makes stepping go towards smaller indices.
quote: Negative i and j are interpreted as n + i and n + j where n is the number of elements in the corresponding dimension. Negative k makes stepping go towards smaller indices.

claim: as_strided applies exactly the strides and shape it is given, so incorrect ones can make elements point to invalid memory and corrupt results or crash the program.
quote: as_strided creates a view into the array given the exact strides and shape. This means it manipulates the internal data structure of ndarray and, if done incorrectly, the array elements can point to invalid memory and can corrupt results or crash your program. It is advisable to always use the original x.strides when calculating new strides to avoid reliance on a contiguous memory layout.

claim: With order='C', reshape reads elements from the input and places them in the output in C index order, in which the last axis index changes fastest and the first axis index slowest.
quote: Read the elements of a using this index order, and place the elements into the reshaped array using this index order. ‘C’ means to read / write the elements using C-like index order, with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first axis index changing slowest.

locator: numpy.reshape, parameter order, note after the 'F' description
claim: The 'C' and 'F' order options refer only to index order and take no account of the array's memory layout.
quote: Note that the ‘C’ and ‘F’ options take no account of the memory layout of the underlying array, and only refer to the order of indexing.

claim: NumPy attempts a no-copy reshape when the array is not contiguous in the requested order, and if that attempt succeeds it uses the computed strides instead of copying.
The no-copy attempt grows a run of new axes and a run of old axes until their extent products are equal, and only then checks whether those old axes can be combined.
